title: Tolerance Stack-Up Analysis
summary: Worst-case and statistical (RSS) tolerance stack analysis of dimension chains to guarantee assembly fit and function.

sections.heading: Why Stacks Matter
sections.content:
Every dimension on a drawing carries a tolerance, and tolerances **accumulate** along chains of parts. A stack-up analysis answers: *what is the worst (or likely) gap, interference, or total dimension when all tolerances combine?* — the question that decides whether a bearing seat actually holds, whether a cover closes, or whether a shaft engages its coupling.

Skipping the analysis is the classic cause of parts that pass inspection individually but fail as an assembly — each component in spec, the product out of spec.

sections.heading: Building the Dimension Chain
sections.content:
A stack-up starts with a **loop diagram**: draw the chain of dimensions from one reference surface to the other, through every part in the assembly, including the closing (resultant) dimension you care about.

Rules for a clean loop:

- Define a **positive direction** around the loop; dimensions opposing it are negative.
- Convert every dimension to **bilateral ± form** before summing (e.g. 20 +0.1/+0.2 becomes 20.15 ± 0.05; a limit dimension like 10.0 max becomes nominal with one-sided tolerance only if treated as such).
- Include **all** contributors: machined lengths, manufactured thicknesses, part seating shifts, and thermal growth if the operating range is wide.
- Name the **closing dimension** — the gap or interference the design actually cares about — it is never a drawn dimension.

sections.heading: Worst-Case Method
sections.content:
The **worst-case (WC) method** assumes every tolerance arrives at its extreme simultaneously. The total is simply the sum of absolute tolerances, and the nominal is the sum of nominals:

$$T_{WC} = \sum |t_i|$$

Example — three parts stacked to a closing height:

| Part | Nominal ± tol (mm) |
|---|---|
| Housing | 20 ± 0.10 |
| Spacer | 30 ± 0.20 |
| Cover | 10 ± 0.15 |

Nominal total = 60 mm;  $T_{WC} = 0.10 + 0.20 + 0.15 = 0.45$ mm → closing dimension **60 ± 0.45 mm**.

WC guarantees 100% assembly — every pair of parts fits, always. The cost is tight individual tolerances. Use WC when failure is unacceptable (safety-critical, hard interference, one-of-a-kind) or when part counts are small.

sections.heading: Statistical (RSS) Method
sections.content:
The **root-sum-square (RSS)** method recognizes that independent processes rarely hit extremes together. Assuming each tolerance band holds ±3σ and tolerances are independent and centered, the combined band is:

$$T_{RSS} = \sqrt{\sum t_i^2}$$

For the same three parts:  $T_{RSS} = \sqrt{0.10^2 + 0.20^2 + 0.15^2} = \sqrt{0.0725} = 0.269$ mm → closing dimension **60 ± 0.269 mm**.

The RSS result is about **40% tighter** than worst case — identical design, looser (cheaper) part tolerances. The trade: a small fraction of assemblies (roughly 0.27% beyond ±3σ combined) may not fit, so RSS is chosen where a rework or selective-assembly strategy exists, or where many parts make WC absurdly conservative. Since real processes shift and are not perfectly centered, many organizations apply RSS with a **safety factor (1.5–2)** or use Monte-Carlo simulation when part distributions are known.

sections.heading: GD&T & MMC in Stacks
sections.content:
Coordinate tolerances treat size and location independently; GD&T lets them interact. For a hole controlled with position at **maximum material condition**, the effective location tolerance grows by the bonus as the hole departs from MMC:

$$T_{bonus} = D_{actual} - D_{MMC}$$

so the **virtual condition** (worst-case mating boundary) of a hole is $VC = D_{MMC} - T_{spec}$. When a stack-up involves GD&T-controlled features, include the **worst-case virtual condition** in WC analysis — it is the correct boundary for mating. Floating vs fixed fastener cases also change how the closing gap is computed; derive the loop from the assembly function, not from the drawing layout.

sections.heading: Practical Stack-Up Tips
sections.content:
Field experience with stacks, condensed:

- **Walk the shortest path** — the closing dimension should pass through the fewest contributors; redesign can shorten the chain and loosen every tolerance.
- **Keep a spreadsheet discipline** — named contributors, formula cells, and a clearly flagged closing dimension make the analysis auditable in review.
- **Convert everything to bilateral first** — asymmetric tolerances hide bias; restating them as ± exposes the true nominal.
- **Watch out for repeated features** — bearing clearances, bolt-hole patterns, and gasket stacks multiply nominals even though tolerances add linearly.
- **Validate with a trial build** — a physical stack of as-produced parts remains the ground truth; feed measured distributions back into RSS inputs (see [[quality-control-and-spc|SPC]].

keyTakeaways: Tolerances accumulate: always analyze the dimension chain for the closing dimension.
Worst-case (sum of tolerances) guarantees fit but tightens parts; RSS (sqrt of sum of squares) loosens parts but accepts a small non-fit tail.
Convert all dimensions to bilateral ± form before summing.
Use virtual condition (MMC/GD&T) for mating boundaries, and validate stacks with a real trial build.
